# The merge layer, the queue layer and the tiers

This is the guide of the gates part for the two layers that sit after the file layout of the architecture guide: what happens when two changes that both touch a generated file meet (the merge layer), and how a stream of changes is proved and landed so that each is not proved again for every other one that lands first (the queue layer). It backs gates.protection.3, gates.protection.5, gates.command.15 and gates.command.17 to .21, and rests on arch.structure.9 and the shared-files chapter in the architecture guide. A source key in parentheses names a tool that does the same thing; the keys are in `sources.yaml`. Words a cold reader may not know are in the glossary at the end.

## 1. What the file layout does not fix

After the architecture guide’s layout, two changes that touch disjoint files rebase without a conflict and keep their verdicts. But a rebase is a new tree, and a new tree is a new proof: the stamp a passing tier writes is keyed to the tree’s id, and a landing step that wants the head rebased on the base moves the base under everything queued. With about a hundred landings in three days, a proof of two to three minutes each is the floor. The merge layer decides who resolves a conflict that is left. The queue layer decides how many proofs a stream of changes costs.

## 2. The merge layer: who resolves a conflict in a generated file

The answer is the landing step, by regenerating, and not git, a driver or a builder. Four mechanisms were weighed and three refused.

- **A merge driver in the builders’ clones: no.** A custom driver is defined in the clone’s own configuration, never in the repository (git-gitattributes: the definition is done in `.git/config`, not in the attributes file). It would have to be installed in every builder’s clone, and a builder’s clone is exactly where the gate’s trust model puts no trust. A driver that runs the generators from the head’s own tree is a change judging itself.
- **The union merge: no.** It keeps both sides’ added lines "in random order and the user should verify the result" (git-gitattributes). Nothing a check reads can be union-merged: a registry in YAML, a sorted list a parser checks, a source file. The one safe use is an append-only log nothing parses, and a repository that has followed the architecture guide has none it wants.
- **Recorded resolutions: no.** `rerere` records a clone’s own hand resolutions and replays them (git-rerere). It helps a person who resolves the same conflict twice; it does nothing across clones, and it would silently replay the resolution of a hand-written file.
- **The attribute that marks a file generated: yes, for what it does.** The attribute hides the file’s diff by default on the hosting site so reviewers read the source (github-linguist-generated). It changes nothing about merging. Extend it to every generated output. Note that the attributes file is itself read by the archive the landing check is built from, so a change to it is a change to the judge and needs a verdict.

What replaces the builder’s rebase for generated files is the landing step (gates.protection.5).

## 3. Regenerate at landing: the four safety properties

When a candidate conflicts only in files a generator owns, the landing step takes the base side, runs the generators, commits the result as its own commit, and proves the result. That is safe because of four properties, and a landing step that lacks one should refuse to regenerate.

1. **The owned-paths list comes from the base’s generators, not the head’s.** A command of the generators prints the paths they write, and the landing step builds that command from the base revision, as it already builds the judge. The head cannot add a path to the list that judges it.
2. **Regenerate only when every conflicting path is owned, and a regenerate never changes a hand-written file.** One hand-written path in the conflict set returns the whole candidate to its builder with the paths named. Beyond the conflict set: if running the generators on the merged tree would alter any path they do not own, the landing fails. A generator that rewrites a hand file is a bug in the generator, and the change that introduced it is what returns.
3. **The regenerated tree is a new tree and gets the full proof.** The stamp is keyed to the tree id, so nothing is served from either side’s stamp: the generated-file check and the whole tier run on the merged, regenerated tree. That is what makes "take either side, then regenerate" safe: the side taken does not matter, because the generators overwrite it, and the proof decides.
4. **A protected generated path keeps its verdict, and landing never writes one.** A generated file can also be protected, such as the landing check’s own closure list. If the regenerated bytes are not covered by a verdict the base already holds, the landing fails with the path and the digest, and whoever dispatches the work asks for the verdict.

Until the landing step does this itself, the same procedure by hand has a person or a merge agent as the driver. The one thing to add now: record, in the note of the train, that the resolution was generated-only, so a later look can tell a regenerated landing from a hand-resolved one.

## 4. The queue layer

**Batching is the first tool and is cheap.** One train of N changes is one proof for N. Trains of two or three changes land five changes on two proofs. Cap a train at the budget of the tier: a candidate that would push the tier past its budget is split. Batching also tells you who to blame: a train that fails is bisected, as tide and bors do (tide-batches, bors-ng-batches).

**Speculative trains, "prove ahead", pay only with a spare runner.** Zuul tests change N on top of changes 1 to N-1 "with the assumption they pass" and, when one fails, tests the rest again without it (zuul-gating). GitHub’s merge queue builds queue branches that include the changes ahead and recreates them when one fails (github-merge-queue). Mergify runs up to a set number of parallel batches (mergify-parallel-checks). All three buy wall time by spending a runner. The cheap form is: while train n is in its landing check and push, build train n+1’s candidate on train n’s expected tree and start its proof; if train n fails, discard the proof and rebuild n+1 on the base. In steady state that saves one proof per train and costs one wasted proof per failed train.

**When each pays.**

- Batch from the start. It needs no spare runner.
- Prove ahead only when the queue regularly holds two or more trains, a second runner is idle, and fewer than about one train in ten fails. If most failures are conflicts and verdict misses, fix those first: the file layout and the regenerate remove them, and speculation on a queue that fails one in five is a coin toss.

**What not to do.**

- Do not key the stamp to anything looser than the tree id to make a rebased proof reusable. A stamp is a claim, not a proof, and a stamp that survives a rebase is a stamp over a tree nobody ran.
- Do not accept a merge commit at landing to avoid the rebase. The check that the head is rebased on the base is what lets the base’s list judge the head’s diff.

## 5. Trade-offs

- **A generated-only resolution hides a bad merge until the proof.** Two changes that each add a generated row by hand, against the rule, are "resolved" by the generators discarding both. That is acceptable: the generated-file check fails if their source is missing, and nobody edits the output.
- **A landing step that regenerates is a writer of files.** It already writes generated outputs; the lock file of issued ids is one more if rule ids are assigned at landing. A provisional id must be refused on the main branch, or a half-assigned rule could land.
- **Prove-ahead needs a dispatcher that tracks two candidates**, and wastes a proof per failed train. Its gain is one proof per train, and with the file work done it is the only lever left.
- **The attribute that marks generated files hides diffs.** Reviewers read the source, not the output, so the source must be where the change is visible.

## 6. Landing a train, in short

1. Gather the approved changes whose files are disjoint or whose conflicts are all generated. Cap at the tier’s budget.
2. Rebase the train once on the base. If the only conflicts are in generated files, regenerate; if any hand-written path conflicts, return that change to its builder.
3. Run the generated-file check and the tier once on the resulting tree. Nothing is served from a stamp of either side.
4. Check that every protected path in the result has a verdict the base already holds. A missing verdict fails the landing with the digest; landing never writes one.
5. Land, and note in the train’s record whether the resolution was generated-only.

## 7. The tiers by moment, and how the members run

The tests guide holds the handbook for a project starting out: which moment holds what, and the numbers that ruled it. The gate side of it is five points, and each is a rule.

1. **Six moments (gates.command.17).** Commit runs the check-only members in seconds. Push runs the whole gate within its budget. Review asks whether an independent reader accepts it, in one round or two. Landing proves the candidate once. Release adds only what proves a release: the crash-injection run and the reproducible-build dry run. On demand holds the long fuzz run and the heavy race run, which block nothing.
2. **Members at the same time (gates.command.18).** A pool runs the members, and a member that reads what another writes declares `after` it. The measured push kept 1.7 of 15 CPUs busy while it ran fourteen members one after another. The report is printed as the serial one was, cheapest first, and the stamp and the budget do not change.
3. **Tools by pin (gates.command.19).** The check is the guard and runs once per run; the install is the fix and runs when the check fails or a pin file changed.
4. **A busy-share report (gates.command.20).** The gate prints how many CPUs it kept busy beside its wall time, and a small share is a finding. A run that passed only under the loaded-host clause is a finding, unjudged and never counted green, and it is printed at the top (tests.measures.9).
5. **A fresh clone passes (gates.command.21).** After the documented setup, every member passes in a clone made from the remote, with each ordering between members declared.

Two more things belong to the gate side. The lint step allows parallel runners on the one shared cache, so it never fails or waits on another lint (gates.command.22), and it lands with the parallel members. And a ruling makes these rules the one test execution strategy of every project: the same three tiers, the same kinds of member, and a project differs only in its member list, with any other difference a recorded exemption with an expiry. The tier runner is shared code that every project runs (#642 holds its design note), so a rule here is a rule of that runner and not of five copies of it.

Two rules are proposed and wait for the owner: a lighter hook for a builder (gates.hooks.8) and test selection at push (tests.selection.16), which the hook follows. The pre-push hook stays the whole tier until they are decided (gates.hooks.1, gates.hooks.4).

## 8. The development cycle: the gate side of the handbook

The tests guide (its sections 6 to 10) holds the handbook of the Development Cycle Standard, as adopted: the six moments with their questions and budgets, the forty-four core rules by moment, how a stack adds lines, the mistakes ranked by cost, and the checklist for a new project. This section holds the gate side of it: what the runner, the hook, the landing step and the registry must do, each as a rule of this part.

### The six moments, from the gate's side

| Moment | The question | What the gate does | Budget |
|---|---|---|---|
| Commit | Is what I staged well formed? | The pre-commit hook runs the check-only members: format, generated files, the secrets scan of the staged diff against a reviewed allowlist, the supply config, the protected-path check. Nothing writes (gates.command.28). | Seconds |
| Push | Does this tree pass everything a push must? | The pre-push hook calls the runner and nothing else (gates.hooks.9). The runner runs every member at once in a pool capped at cores divided by slots (gates.command.18, gates.command.27), installs a tool only when its pin changed (gates.command.19, gates.command.24), prints each member's count and the CPU share beside the wall time (gates.measures.6, gates.command.20), and lists every member that cannot run here as SKIPPED with its cause (gates.command.30). | The measured floor times 1.5 (tests.measures.10) |
| Review | Would an independent reader accept it? | No members. A reviewer who did not write it, fix rounds on the delta, each new guard broken by hand, a verdict on every protected path (agents.review.1 to .7, gates.protection.1 to .3). Rounds are counted (gates.measures.5). | One round, two at most |
| Land | Does the merged candidate pass, once? | The landing step gathers approved, disjoint changes as a train, proves the merged tree once with the proof keyed to the candidate tree, makes one push, and builds the next train on this train's squash (gates.land.16). The judge is built from the base (gates.land.17). A skip is red here (gates.command.30), and a red names the last green main (gates.land.18). | One proof per train |
| Release | Does it prove a release? | The push tier plus the release members, all at once, on a fresh clone of the tag, on every claimed platform (gates.command.16), with the secrets scan over all history. The stamp is not taken as proof (gates.land.15). A tag push from a hosted workflow does not run the local hook (gates.hooks.9). | Push plus about 30 seconds, from the floor |
| On demand | What do the deep runs find? | Each run is a row of the members file with the tier on demand, logged where the hub reads it, and a red opens an issue the same day (gates.command.26). The heavy race run is the hub's daily run on the main branch. | Minutes, blocks nothing |

Wall time is from the first member's start to the last member's end; the wait for a slot and the time the slot was held print on their own lines (gates.measures.7). A heavy run takes a slot and a light command runs bare, with landings ahead in the queue (gates.command.29). Each moment has an owner, and nobody runs a later moment's tier as their hand-in (gates.command.31).

### The core rules the gate holds

Of the forty-four core rules, these are the gate's: C1 (gates.command.23), C2 (gates.command.18, gates.command.12), C3 (gates.command.17, gates.command.3), C5 (gates.command.20), C6 (gates.command.19, gates.command.24), C7 (gates.command.21), C8 (gates.command.16), C9 (gates.command.22, gates.command.25), C10 (gates.land.15), C11 (gates.hooks.9 with gates.hooks.1, .4 and .5), C12 (gates.command.26), C13 (gates.measures.1), C14 (gates.command.27), C15 (gates.measures.6), C16 (gates.command.28), C17 (gates.measures.7), C18 (gates.command.29), C20 (gates.command.30), C21 (gates.command.31), C22 (gates.ratchets.1, gates.ratchets.4), R3 (gates.land.16), R4 (gates.land.17), R5 (gates.land.12), R6 (gates.measures.5) and R8 (gates.land.18). The test rules (T1 to T12) and the review rules (R1, R2, R7) are in the tests and agents parts, and the tests guide's section 7 maps all forty-four.

### How a stack adds members

A stack adds members to these moments and never a moment of its own. Its lines are rows of the same members file, with the same fields: tier, kind, cost, weight, platform, network need and any member they run after (gates.command.23). A stack member that misses its moment's budget moves to the next blocking moment, never to a timer (gates.command.17). Its tools take their workers and cache from the pool (gates.command.25). A stack member that needs a browser, a runtime or the network declares it and prints SKIPPED where the host lacks it, and that skip is red at land and release unless a dated exemption names the machine (gates.command.30). The stack's own part of the rulebook holds its lines.

### The mistakes the gate rules prevent

Ranked by cost, from the tests guide's table (its section 9), the rows that a gate rule stops: slot waits logged only at their start and light commands in heavy slots (gates.measures.7, gates.command.29: at least 2,846 agent-minutes in two days); the full tier run bare as the hand-in (gates.command.31: 198 gates, 25.3 slot-hours in a day); every waiting green re-proved when the main branch moved (gates.land.16, gates.land.15: 470 land-wall minutes that landed nothing); a red post-land proof with no main named (gates.land.18: 333 agent-minutes); deep runs kept in the release tier (gates.command.17: 27 minutes 47 seconds); a serial gate with a cold single-threaded lint (gates.command.18, gates.command.25: 394 of 607 seconds); logic in the hook (gates.hooks.9: 374 of 391 seconds); a hosted backstop after every landing (gates.land.16: 633 seconds median, holding a slot); a green with no counts (gates.measures.6: 20 spec files unrun for 4 days 20 hours); self-triggering workflows (supply.workflows.1: 5,000 hosted minutes in 5 days); a fresh clone red (gates.command.21: 14 of 38 repositories); the loaded-host clause excusing every run (tests.measures.9, tests.measures.10); a tag push re-firing the hook (gates.hooks.9: 403 seconds over four publishes); lint refusing itself (gates.command.22: seven refused pushes in a week); tools reinstalled every push (gates.command.19, gates.command.24); uncapped workers (gates.command.27); a skip read as a failure (gates.command.30: 49 of 49 blocks); a run nobody watched (gates.command.26); a platform claimed and never run (gates.command.16); and a push past the hook (gates.hooks.5).

### A new project, the gate steps

1. Pin the shared runner and write the members file, every member with its tier, kind, cost, weight, platform and network need (gates.command.23, gates.command.30).
2. Install the hooks: pre-commit runs the check-only members, pre-push calls the runner for the push tier and nothing else, and the deny refuses every bypass (gates.hooks.2, gates.hooks.9, gates.hooks.5).
3. Put every tool, browser and image behind a pin and one check (gates.command.19, gates.command.24).
4. Run the push tier on a fresh clone on every claimed platform and read its counts (gates.command.21, gates.command.16, gates.measures.6).
5. Measure the floor on a quiet host and set the budgets at 1.5 times it (tests.measures.10); the report prints wall time, queue wait and slot hold apart (gates.measures.7).
6. Where the project has protected paths, build the judge from the base and name the verdict's home (gates.land.17, gates.protection.2).
7. Land trains, proved once, keyed to the candidate tree, one push each (gates.land.16).
8. Name every on-demand run in the members file with where its log goes (gates.command.26).
9. Where a rule meets existing breakage, register a shrink-only baseline with an owner (gates.ratchets.1, gates.ratchets.4).

## Glossary

- **Base, head:** the main branch at landing, and the change being landed.
- **Moment:** one of the six points of the cycle (commit, push, review, land, release, on demand), each with one question and one budget.
- **Slot:** a share of a shared host that a heavy run takes before it starts; the pool's capacity is the cores divided by the slots.
- **Stamp:** a record that a tier passed on one exact tree, keyed to the tree’s id; it is a claim to skip a repeat run, not a proof for any other tree.
- **Tier:** a named set of checks run at one point (for example before a push), with a time budget.
- **Proof:** the full run of the checks on the exact tree that will land.
- **Train:** several approved changes landed together, proved once.
- **Verdict:** a record, kept in the repository, that an independent reviewer read a protected file at one exact content and accepted it.
- **Protected path:** a file or folder, or a pattern with one star segment, whose change needs a verdict because it can weaken a check.
- **Landing step, landing check:** the trusted code that moves a reviewed change onto the main branch, built from the base and run on the head.
- **Judge, judge file, closure list:** the judge is the trusted program, built from the base, that decides whether a change may land. A judge file is a file it is built from, and the closure list names them; a change to one is protected like a golden.
- **Generator-owned path:** a file a generator in the repository’s own tools writes and the generated-file check holds.
- **Merge driver, union merge, rerere:** git’s ways of resolving a content conflict by program: a configured command, keeping both sides, and replaying a recorded resolution.
